value.overview: The Black-crowned Tityra is a medium-sized tropical bird of the tityra family, found from southern Mexico through Central America and across much of northern and eastern South America. It is usually associated with forest edges, clearings, river corridors, plantations, and other partly open wooded habitats. Often seen perched high in the canopy, it feeds on fruit and large insects. In Costa Rica it is an uncommon, local species that can be overlooked because it spends much of its time above the canopy.
value.classification: The Black-crowned Tityra belongs to the family Tityridae, a Neotropical group that includes tityras, becards, and related birds. Its scientific name is Tityra inquisitor.
value.identification: Adults are compact, broad-headed birds with a stout, hooked bill. The male has a mostly gray body, black wings and tail, a dark crown and face, and a conspicuous pale patch around the bill and cheek. Females and immature birds are browner and less strongly marked, and may be confused with female Masked Tityras. The species is generally smaller and more contrastingly patterned than the Masked Tityra. Its high, exposed perches and slow, deliberate movements are useful field clues.
value.rangeHabitat: The Black-crowned Tityra ranges from southern Mexico through most of Central America and widely across tropical South America. In Costa Rica it is widespread but fairly uncommon and local, occurring in suitable areas on both slopes, especially in lowlands and foothills. It uses humid and seasonally drier evergreen forest, second growth, forest borders, tall woodland, river-edge vegetation, plantations, and clearings with mature trees. It is usually found from sea level to roughly 1,200 meters, although its exact upper limit varies regionally.
value.migrationStatus: It is generally considered resident or only locally mobile, not a regular long-distance migrant. In Costa Rica it occurs throughout the year, although local abundance may vary seasonally and some records are concentrated during the March–June breeding period.
value.breeding: Breeding information is best documented from Central America. The species nests in tree cavities, including old woodpecker holes and natural hollows, and may also use other enclosed cavities in large trees. Both adults participate in nest-related activities, and the nest is typically placed high above the ground. The female lays a small clutch of pale eggs with darker markings, and the young are fed largely on animal prey. Breeding in Costa Rica has been reported mainly during the first half of the year.
value.dietFeeding: The diet includes small and medium-sized fruits, berries, and large insects. Adults commonly sit quietly in the canopy or along an edge before making short flights to pick fruit or seize prey from foliage and branches. Insects are especially important when feeding nestlings. By consuming and carrying fruit between trees, the species may contribute to seed dispersal in tropical forests and wooded agricultural landscapes.
value.behavior: Black-crowned Tityras are usually encountered singly or in pairs and often remain conspicuously perched near the top of a tree. They can be territorial and may chase other birds from favored perches or feeding sites. Their flight is typically short and direct between nearby trees. They are not strongly associated with mixed-species feeding flocks, preferring to forage independently in the upper layers of forest and woodland.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered to be decreasing, although the species remains widespread and has a large overall range.
